grid_cell: Kernel code × Performance eng.; Scheduling × CI & release (L-lkp)
problem_statement: Developers receive automated performance-regression reports from the kernel test robot but cannot tell which ones are real and caused by the blamed commit; many are noise or misattributed, and most get no visible follow-up.
who_suffers: patch authors and maintainers; the robot operators
evidence_1_quote: 0day bot has reported many strange kernel performance changes that the bisected culprit commits have nothing to do with the benchmark, which make patch authors confused or even annoyed.
evidence_2_quote: I do see *some* regression in my setup, but the data is very noisy, so I'm not sure I can confirm it.
evidence_2_type: practice (LKML 2021, patch author replying to a robot report; quoted inside the message)
evidence_3_quote: A great portion of them may also be random noises (eg. performance fluctuations).
frequency_indicator: oe-lkp archive: 979 robot performance-regression reports 2016-2026; 73 (7.5%) cited by a mainline fix/revert; 569 (58%) with no human reply (tools/probes, 2026-11-05); extra practice item: https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/2403.0/03148.html "This _looks_ like noise to me." (2024) and robot FAQ "you are not obliged to respond to a robot"
cost_indicator: developer time and confusion ("confused or even annoyed"); unacted real regressions ship
evidence_score: 10 (4 independent practice items ×2 — LPC 2021, LKML 2017/2021/2024 — + recurring 2017-2024 +1 + cost +1)

problem_statement: Kernel developers receive duplicate or overlapping automated reports for the same underlying problem.
evidence_1_quote: Most of the test "regressions" may be duplicates to each other (eg. a bug in mainline kernel will also show up in various developer trees).
evidence_2_quote: A significant number of reported duplicates was one of common complaints.
evidence_3_quote: So this is just noise. And enough noise means that signal is lost.
frequency_indicator: oe-lkp: 6,517 blamed commits, only 226 with >1 separate report (robot already groups tests per commit); 598 non-perf signatures blamed on >1 commit
cost_indicator: triage effort; signal lost in noise

problem_statement: Some reported kernel regressions are never resolved, especially when nobody identifies the change that caused them, and reports to the top maintainer often get no reply.
who_suffers: users who hit regressions; regression tracker; maintainers
evidence_1_quote: Nearly all of them are, as long as the change causing the regression (the “culprit commit”) is reliably identified. Some regressions can be fixed without this, but often it’s required.
evidence_2_quote: unlikely to be resolved because nobody is able to find the culprit in reasonable time
evidence_3_quote: his reports to Torvalds on open regressions often get no reply at all
cost_indicator: unfixed regressions reach users; tracker workload
evidence_score: 5 (all three items trace to the same tracker maintainer, so counted as 2 independent by time period ×2 + recurring +1)

grid_cell: Kernel code × Maintenance & evolution (K12 + kernel git)
problem_statement: Fixes for tracked regressions often do not link to the regression report, so the tracker and maintainers must connect them by hand.
evidence_1_quote: There's no link to the actual problem the patch fixes.
evidence_1_type: practice (kernel process docs, quoting a 2022 mail from the top maintainer)
evidence_2_quote: Maintainers can also simply fail to notice that a patch fixes a regression, he said
frequency_indicator: regzbot resolved entries: ~490 matched automatically via Link/Closes vs ~1,562 with a manual "fix:" command (heuristic parse)
cost_indicator: manual tracking workload (see LWN 990599 on tracker funding)
